issues.legal_issue: A non-political lease that passed to a successor state remained valid and enforceable despite the asserted lapse of earlier political arrangements.
material_facts: The original lease was made for a long term between the ruler of an Indian State and the Secretary of State for India in Council for the purposes of the Province of Madras.
Section 177 of the Government of India Act, 1935 treated the Province of Madras as the lessee under the existing lease.
There was no unambiguous denouncement of the lease after the Indian Independence Act, 1947 came into force.
The successor governments entered into supplemental agreements that expressly proceeded on the basis that the lease continued.
issues.conclusion: The lease remained valid and binding on the successor state and was enforceable by the plaintiff; the defendant was estopped from asserting that it had lapsed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 177 of the Government of India Act, 1935 transferred the relevant existing contract to the Province of Madras. Section 7(1)(b) of the Indian Independence Act, 1947 concerned political treaties and agreements, not an ordinary lease, and denouncement under its proviso had to be express and unequivocal. Articles 294(b) and 295(2) of the Constitution provided for succession to the relevant rights and obligations. Mullaperiyar Environmental Protection Forum v. Union of India treated the lease as non-political; Babu Ram Saksena v. State and State of Himachal Pradesh v. Union of India were distinguished. State of Andhra Pradesh v. State of Maharashtra supported the view that inter-state agreements are entered into with competent legal and technical assistance.

predicates.ordinary_lease_for_provincial_purposes: The contracting parties made an ordinary lease for purposes that became purposes of a province.
predicates.successor_state_assumed_contractual_righ: A successor government assumed the rights and obligations attached to the lease.
predicates.successor_states_executed_supplemental_a: The successor governments executed later agreements that recognized the continued lease.
predicates.not_express_post_independence_denounceme: The ruler did not expressly and unequivocally denounce the lease after the relevant independence legislation took effect.

issues.definition: When an ordinary provincial-purpose lease passes to a successor government, and it has not been expressly denounced but is recognized in later agreements, the lease remains binding and enforceable.

issues.legal_issue: A state-to-state suit based on an ordinary, non-political agreement is maintainable under the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction and is not excluded by the treaty proviso.
material_facts: The suit was brought by one State against another and raised a dispute involving the existence of legal rights and the constitutional validity of legislation.
The claim relied in part on an ordinary lease agreement rather than a political settlement.
The principal challenge also concerned the validity of state legislation.
issues.conclusion: The suit was maintainable under Article 131, and the proviso to that Article did not bar the claim based on the lease.
issues.legal_principle: Article 131 confers original jurisdiction over qualifying disputes between States involving legal rights. Its proviso, like Article 363, excludes disputes concerning political instruments, not ordinary non-political agreements. Mullaperiyar Environmental Protection Forum v. Union of India had also held that the lease was an ordinary, non-political agreement.

predicates.state_to_state_legal_rights_dispute: Two or more States are in dispute over a question on which the existence or extent of a legal right depends.
predicates.claim_based_on_ordinary_nonpolitical_agr: A claim in the dispute is based on an ordinary agreement rather than a political instrument.

issues.definition: A state-to-state dispute involving legal rights may proceed in the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction when its agreement-based claim arises from an ordinary, non-political agreement.

issues.legal_issue: A final decision on an issue directly contested between the same States in an earlier constitutional proceeding operates as res judicata in their later suit.
material_facts: In an earlier proceeding between the same States, the safety of the dam at the proposed higher water level was directly contested.
The Court considered evidence and expert reports and permitted the water level to be raised to the level it found safe.
The earlier judgment became final after a review petition was dismissed.
The later suit raised the same safety issue between the same States.
issues.conclusion: The earlier judgment operated as res judicata on the safety issue, and the defendant could not re-agitate the issues already decided.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, including Explanation VIII, expresses the public-policy rule of res judicata. A decision in a proceeding under Article 32 or Article 226 can bind the parties in a later suit. The Court relied on Duchess of Kingston, Sheoparsan Singh v. Ramnandan Prashad Narayan Singh, Daryao v. State of U.P., Gulab Chand Chhotalal Parikh v. State of Bombay, Union of India v. Nanak Singh, and State of Punjab v. Bua Das Kaushal. A final safety finding may be reconsidered by the Court in changed circumstances, but not displaced unilaterally by a legislature; N.D. Jayal v. Union of India was read consistently with that principle.

predicates.later_suit_between_same_parties: The parties to a later suit are the same as, or claim under the same titles as, the parties to an earlier proceeding.
predicates.same_issue_directly_decided_in_prior_pro: The issue in the later suit was directly and substantially contested and decided in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.prior_decision_final: The earlier decision became final and was not set aside in an available review process.

issues.definition: When the same parties bring a later suit over an issue directly decided in a final earlier proceeding, that issue is barred from being litigated again.

issues.legal_issue: A legislature cannot, by a law directed at a final judicial finding on disputed facts, reverse that finding without changing the legal basis on which the judgment rested.
material_facts: The Court had heard the two States and determined on evidence that the dam was safe at the approved water level.
Soon after that judgment, the defendant State amended its legislation to designate the dam as endangered, limit its water level, and authorize a state authority to regulate or restrict its operation.
The amendment directly contradicted the earlier factual determination and sought to prevent implementation of the judgment.
The amendment did not validate a defective law or remove a defect identified by the Court.
issues.conclusion: The amendment was unconstitutional and ultra vires in its application to the dam, and the rights crystallized by the earlier judgment could not be nullified by legislation.
issues.legal_principle: The separation of powers is an entrenched constitutional principle and a component of the rule of law and Article 14. Under Articles 245 and 246, a legislature may enact a valid law that changes the basis of a judgment within its competence, but it cannot simply reverse a judicial finding or direct the disregard of a final decision. A validating law must be within legislative competence and remove the defect identified by the court; it must also comply with Part III. The Court relied on Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality, Janapada Sabha Chhindwara v. Central Provinces Syndicate Ltd., Mahal Chand Sethia v. State of West Bengal, Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India, P. Sambamurthy v. State of A.P., Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal, Re, People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India, I.N. Saksena v. State of Madhya Pradesh, P. Kannadasan v. State of T.N., Indian Aluminium Company v. State of Kerala, Arooran Sugars Ltd. v. State of T.N., and I.R. Coelho v. State of T.N. The relevant amendment provisions included Sections 62 and 62A of the amended Kerala Act.

rule.if: state_to_state_dispute and final_judicial_finding_on_contested_facts and later_unilateral_law_contradicts_finding and no_fundamental_change_to_judgment_basis

predicates.state_to_state_dispute: The dispute is between governments of different States.
predicates.final_judicial_finding_on_contested_fact: A court reached a final finding on disputed facts after hearing the parties and considering evidence.
predicates.later_unilateral_law_contradicts_finding: One party later enacted a law that contradicts the final finding and impedes its implementation.
predicates.no_fundamental_change_to_judgment_basis: The later law does not fundamentally alter the legal basis on which the earlier judgment was decided.

issues.definition: When one State responds to a final factual determination in a state-to-state dispute with a unilateral law that contradicts it without changing the judgment’s basis, the law is unconstitutional as applied.

issues.legal_issue: A final finding on dam safety is not reopened when later evidence does not establish a material change in circumstances.
material_facts: The earlier judgment had found the dam safe at the permitted water level after considering expert material.

The Court later appointed an Empowered Committee to investigate hydrologic, structural, and seismic safety, with technical studies carried out through specialist organizations and with representatives of both States involved.
The Committee found the dam safe and concluded that the concerns raised did not establish a need to depart from the earlier finding.
The Court found no change in circumstances or emergent situation warranting reopening the safety issue.
issues.conclusion: The earlier safety finding remained controlling; the evidence did not justify reopening it, and the dam was found safe for restoration of the approved level, subject to the specified strengthening, monitoring, and supervision.
issues.legal_principle: A final judicial finding may be reconsidered by the Court itself if a substantial change in circumstances is shown, but it cannot be reopened merely by reasserting concerns already determined. The Court referred to N.D. Jayal v. Union of India and applied the finality and res judicata principles described in its discussion of Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It also considered the Empowered Committee’s technical investigations and conclusions.

predicates.prior_final_dam_safety_adjudication: A court finally determined dam safety after hearing the parties and considering evidence.
predicates.later_court_directed_expert_review: The court later obtained expert review and technical investigation of the safety issue.
predicates.no_material_change_in_safety_circumstanc: The later investigation did not establish a material change or emergency that would justify revisiting the earlier finding.

issues.definition: When a court’s later expert review identifies no material change in safety circumstances, its earlier final safety finding remains controlling.

issues.legal_issue: Technical studies obtained by a court-appointed committee may be relied on when the parties’ representatives participate in the investigation process.
material_facts: The Court-appointed committee directed specialist organizations to conduct investigations, tests, and technical studies.
Representatives of both States participated in the committee’s coordination process.
The reports were supplied to the objecting State, although some materials were provided after the committee had submitted its report.
The Court found that the committee had thoroughly examined the safety issues and rejected the objection to its findings.
issues.conclusion: The Court considered the technical studies and relied on the Empowered Committee’s safety findings; the objection to the reports was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The Court-appointed committee was tasked with examining the matter and could receive further evidence it considered appropriate. The Court found that the investigations were carried out in association with both States’ representatives and rejected the contention that the committee’s procedure made the reports unusable or unreliable.

predicates.court_appointed_expert_committee: A court appointed an expert committee to investigate an issue relevant to the proceeding.
predicates.party_representatives_participated_in_in: Representatives of the affected parties participated in the committee’s investigation process.
predicates.reports_disclosed_for_court_consideratio: The resulting technical reports were made available for consideration by the court and parties.

issues.definition: A court may rely on technical reports produced by its expert committee when party representatives participated in the investigation and the reports were available for consideration.

issues.legal_issue: A river is an inter-State river when its basin extends into more than one State, and a State cannot maintain a contrary position inconsistent with its earlier jurisdictional stance and the evidence.
material_facts: The defendant State contended that the river was confined to its territory.
The earlier litigation had involved a jurisdictional objection based on the applicability of the constitutional and statutory inter-State water-dispute framework.
Maps and government publications showed that part of the river basin lay in the other State.
A witness for the defendant acknowledged government material describing the river as inter-State and showing part of its basin in the other State.
issues.conclusion: The defendant could not contend that the river was intra-State; the Court treated it as an inter-State river.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered Article 262 of the Constitution and Section 11 of the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, together with evidence concerning the river basin. The relevant basin includes the river valley, and a portion of the basin in another State is sufficient to establish inter-State status. The Court also relied on the defendant’s earlier jurisdictional position and the evidence before it.

predicates.river_basin_extends_across_state_boundar: Maps or other reliable evidence show that the basin of a river extends into more than one State.
predicates.state_advanced_inconsistent_jurisdiction: A State previously advanced a position concerning inter-State jurisdiction that conflicts with its later claim that the river is confined to one State.

issues.definition: When evidence shows that a river basin extends across State boundaries and a State takes an inconsistent later position, the river is treated as inter-State.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot require a party State to accept a proposed replacement dam without that State’s agreement.
material_facts: The defendant offered to construct a new dam downstream of the existing dam.
The other State rejected the offer.
The Empowered Committee’s proposed alternative contemplated agreement between the States.
issues.conclusion: The proposed new dam could not be imposed on the rejecting State, and the issue was decided against the State making the offer.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that construction of a replacement dam required the agreement of both parties; a proposal for an alternative could not be thrust upon a State that rejected it.

predicates.state_to_state_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute between States.
predicates.replacement_project_proposed_by_one_stat: One State proposes a replacement project as an alternative to an existing arrangement.
predicates.other_state_does_not_agree: The other State rejects or does not agree to the proposed project.

issues.definition: In a dispute between States, one State’s replacement-project proposal cannot be imposed when the other State does not agree.

issues.legal_issue: A permanent injunction may restrain a State from obstructing another State’s established rights when the invasion is substantial and the requested relief is supported by the record.
material_facts: The plaintiff State sought to raise the dam’s water level and carry out repair work permitted by the earlier judgment.
The defendant State’s legislation and conduct threatened to obstruct those rights.
The Court found that water needs in drought-prone areas remained unmet and that the plaintiff had established a substantial invasion of its rights.
The Court found the earlier judgment and safety evidence supported the requested relief.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff was entitled to a permanent injunction restraining the defendant from applying the legislation or otherwise obstructing the approved water-level increase and repair works; a supervisory committee was also constituted to oversee restoration and safety.
issues.legal_principle: In a suit between States, the claimant seeking an injunction must establish a substantial and serious invasion of its rights; an injunction does not follow from every infringement. The Court relied on State of Andhra Pradesh v. State of Maharashtra and found the required substantial invasion established. The Court also provided for supervisory oversight of restoration and safety measures.

predicates.state_to_state_original_suit: The proceeding is an original suit between States.
predicates.substantial_invasion_of_established_righ: The claimant establishes a substantial invasion of a legal right supported by the record.
predicates.threatened_obstruction_of_exercise_of_ri: The opposing State threatens to obstruct the claimant’s exercise of that right.

issues.definition: In an original suit between States, a substantial invasion of an established right coupled with threatened obstruction supports a permanent injunction against the obstruction.
